Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-04
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood Perf), Avery (Lumos Infra), Priya (Lumos ML), Marcus (Lumos SRE), Sasha (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated - may be rough):
Discussed p95/p99 tail sources, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, network hop analysis across VPC peering, KV cache hotkey behavior, batching strategies and quantization options for on-prem runtime. Decided to run targeted bench tests and share configs.

Topics: runtime latency, tail latency, streaming, KV cache TTL, batching window, quantization (4-bit/8-bit), VPC hops, private deployment testing

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros?
[00:12] Avery Brooks: Sure, Avery here, infra lead at Lumos. We're trying to get p99 down from 450ms to under 200ms for our chat endpoint.
[00:20] Priya Singh: Priya, ML eng. We're seeing big tail spikes when customers stream long-ish responses, also non-streaming seems to have different shape.
[00:28] Maya Chen: Maya, principal SE at Redwood. we'll dig into runtime and net path. Carlos will walk through perf numbers later.
[00:35] Marcus Holt: Marcus, SRE. we also want to validate on our air-gapped-ish rack later this quarter.
[01:05] Carlos Rivera: Quick preface — our hypothesis list: 1) KV cache cold misses + hotkey thundering 2) batching windows too large or too small causing head-of-line blocking 3) network serialization across VPC NAT or proxy 4) model quantization path causing occasional kernel fallback.
[01:45] Sasha Ivanov: do you mean kernel fallback as in CPU fallback or different GPU kernel? sometimes it flips to slow kernel and spikes.
[01:52] Carlos Rivera: yeah, we've seen cases where model op layout causes a non-optimized kernel selection, adverse for long sequence lengths.
[02:15] Jordan Patel: to set expectations, we usually separate streaming and non-streaming p95/p99 profiles. streaming adds small per-chunk overhead but helps perceived latency — but if network has extra hops it can amplify tail.
[03:10] Avery Brooks: Our infra: VPC in aws us-west-2, private peering to on-prem lab via transit gateway. An NLB + internal proxy sits in front of the cluster. that's two extra hops.
[03:38] Priya Singh: our token distributions: median 80 tokens, 95th 380, 99th 950. So long tails. We care both about 95 and 99.
[04:00] Maya Chen: big difference. for p99 on 950 tokens you need to watch KV cache sizing and prefix caching. Are you using prefix-level caching or per-request?
[04:14] Priya Singh: prefix cache keyed by prompt hash; we saw some duplication but still quite a few misses.
[04:28] Carlos Rivera: note: KV (we'll sometimes write k-v or K V cache in docs) cache cold misses cost you full forward, which multiplies latency by token count. Also hotkey storms — if many requests reference same prompt variant but slightly different meta, you get cache churn.
[05:05] Marcus Holt: we suspect NAT connection reuse is poor; ephemeral connections triggering TLS renegotiation and adding 30-50ms on the tail sometimes.
[05:28] Jordan Patel: that aligns with us seeing NAT/idle timeouts add spikes. For on-prem we recommend connection pools and keepalive tuning.
[06:00] Carlos Rivera: quick visualization — non-streaming path: request enters -> tokenizer -> full forward with KV lookups -> decode -> return. Streaming: chunked decode, more frequent flushes, more network IO per token. If you have many network hops, streaming amplifies tail because each chunk is an independent packet path.
[06:35] Priya Singh: interesting — so streaming can worsen p99 if network is flaky, but helps perceived latency for median.
[06:48] Maya Chen: Exactly. We often recommend hybrid: stream up to N tokens then switch to non-stream flush for final long tails. That reduces per-chunk overhead for 99th.
[07:20] Sasha Ivanov: what's your view on batching? we have sporadic bursty traffic, thinking about a small batching window to save cost but not hurt latency.
[07:34] Carlos Rivera: batching trades off latency headroom for throughput. For chat with many small requests, micro-batching 10-20ms helps amortize kernel launch. For p99 you need to cap batch depth aggressively because long requests holding GPU can block many small ones.
[08:05] Maya Chen: we have adaptive batching: if queue contains > X requests with similar sequence length, we combine; but we also run preemptive slots to avoid head-of-line. key is throttling long-seq requests onto separate route or model variant.
[08:36] Avery Brooks: route separation — so we could route >512 token requests to dedicated pool? we have reserved nodes for big jobs.
[08:48] Jordan Patel: yes that's a common pattern. dedicate a high-throughput low-parallelism pool for long sequences and a low-latency high-parallelism pool for short chat. Automatic routing policy can fallback if one pool saturated.
[09:20] Priya Singh: what about quantization? we tested 8-bit and sometimes saw 5-10% slower tail due to kernel mismatch.
[09:32] Carlos Rivera: quantization often helps throughput and cost, but QA: some kernels for int8 have lower parallelism depending on architecture. Additionally mixed-precision transitions can cause CPU-GPU synchronization points that spike tail. Test per-model.
[10:05] Marcus Holt: can Redwood provide per-op kernel telemetry? we currently only see high-level GPU utilization in our dashboards.
[10:14] Maya Chen: yes we can surface kernel selector traces and per-op durations in the console (we call it kernel trace export). we'll include example logs in the perf pack.
[10:35] Jordan Patel: quick interjection — we'll want your representative trace samples and a couple of offline prompts so we can reproduce with exact tokenization and sequence lengths.
[10:48] Priya Singh: we'll share a 24h sample and top-50 prompts.
[11:05] Carlos Rivera: network hops — the path through your NLB->proxy->transit->onprem adds serialization and variable queuing. If any hop has a tail (for example proxy's threadpool spike), that shows up at p99. We recommend instrumenting with distributed traces at each hop.
[11:30] Marcus Holt: we do have X-Ray traces but they aggregate; how granular do you need?
[11:38] Maya Chen: per-request at socket accept and TLS handshake and at our runtime ingress/egress. capture tcp_rtt and queuing. For NAT keepalive we recommend setting idle to much longer than your typical inter-request.
[12:05] Jordan Patel: another strategy is KV cache warmers — pre-populate cache for expected prompts during traffic surge windows. but that requires accurate prompt prediction.
[12:26] Priya Singh: we have scheduled campaigns that cause hot keys, yes warming might help.
[12:35] Carlos Rivera: also watch for cache TTLs and shard imbalance. if a shard gets hot, its worker can become a bottleneck and create tail. We suggest sharding keys to distribute evenly.
[13:02] Sasha Ivanov: is there a Redwood tool to re-shard or visualize hot shards?
[13:08] Maya Chen: yes our console shows per-shard hit rates and latency heatmaps. we can share screenshots and the API to pull metrics.
[13:35] Jordan Patel: let's pivot to on-prem specifics — you mentioned air-gapped rack, Marcus?
[13:42] Marcus Holt: yes, it's not fully air-gapped but isolated with strict egress. we plan to run Redwood private. main worry is kernel optimizations for older GPUs and variance in PCIe gen.
[13:58] Carlos Rivera: older GPUs + slower PCIe can increase data movement cost; quantization benefits might be less predictable. For on-prem we recommend model compilation with target arch flags and a small stress test suite.
[14:20] Priya Singh: can Redwood ship compiled kernels for our specific card set?
[14:28] Maya Chen: we can produce tuned builds for supported cards as part of private deployment engagement; it requires sample hardware info and maybe a brief lab run.
[14:45] Carlos Rivera: one more: for tail mitigation we use dynamic preemption — long-running decoding tasks can be preempted at block boundaries to let short requests slip through. It adds complexity but helps p99.
[15:10] Avery Brooks: any open-source dependencies or knobs we should watch? like specific CUDA or driver versions?
[15:20] Carlos Rivera: yes, CUDA minor versions sometimes change kernel perf; keep drivers consistent between nodes. Also enable MPS or use our multi-instance scheduler depending on workload.
[15:48] Jordan Patel: let's look at the test plan we propose — quick steps: 1) reproduce p95/p99 in controlled env 2) isolate KV miss vs network vs kernel 3) tunable test cases for batching windows and streaming chunk size 4) run quantization A/B comparing latency and inference error 5) on-prem lab run to measure PCIe/driver differences.
[16:20] Marcus Holt: sounds good. what's the expected time to get initial bench results?
[16:26] Jordan Patel: with your traces and prompts we can run a first pass in ~3 business days and share results and config snippets.
[16:40] Priya Singh: good. any quick recommendations we can implement now to lower p99?
[16:46] Maya Chen: short term: cap batch size, enable keepalive and connection pooling, increase cache TTL for stable prompts, and route long sequences to the dedicated pool. Those are low-risk.
[17:05] Carlos Rivera: also consider reducing streaming chunk frequency (i.e., larger chunk size) for routes where p99 matters more than perceived streaming immediacy.
[17:24] Sasha Ivanov: can you explain the streaming chunk tradeoff again?
[17:28] Maya Chen: streaming chunk size controls how often you flush a partial decode. smaller chunks = lower median latency but more network roundtrips. For p99 bigger chunks reduce per-token roundtrip overhead. It's workload dependent.
[18:00] Jordan Patel: let's have Carlos run a small simulation with your token distribution to show streaming vs non-streaming p95/p99.
[18:10] Carlos Rivera: will do. we'll simulate NAT timeouts and proxy spikes as part of the model.
[18:25] Priya Singh: what about metrics we should watch in real time?
[18:31] Maya Chen: p50/p95/p99 per route, per-model, tokenization time, KV hit ratio, per-shard queue depth, kernel selection logs, and network RTT at each hop.
[18:52] Jordan Patel: mention of security — you had questions about logging and PII?
[18:56] Avery Brooks: yes, we need to ensure logs don't store raw user data when sending traces to Redwood.
[19:05] Maya Chen: default is sampling + PII redaction; for private deploys you can keep traces local and we operate on hashed prompts. We'll include the security whitepaper and SOC2 details.
[19:30] Marcus Holt: good. back to batching — is there a rule of thumb for batch window vs expected token length?
[19:38] Carlos Rivera: rule of thumb: batch window 5-20ms for chat, increase if dominant tokens per request > 300. But that depends on kernel latency; it's empirical.
[20:00] Priya Singh: are there any safeguards against hotkey thundering?
[20:05] Maya Chen: yes: hotkey queue shaping, backpressure, and explicit warming. Also implement jitter in client-side TTL refresh to avoid synchronized misses.
[20:26] Jordan Patel: quick note on observability rollout — we'll give a sample dashboard with per-route p95/p99, KV hit heatmap, and a trace needle view to find outlier requests.
[20:45] Avery Brooks: thanks, that will be helpful.
[21:00] Carlos Rivera: random note — if you run mixed workloads, consider using separate physical GPUs for long sequences vs short chat to avoid head-of-line.
[21:15] Marcus Holt: separate GPU pools — we can do that with our cluster manager. any scheduling pitfalls?
[21:22] Maya Chen: ensure scheduler labels don't cause noisy neighbor when autoscaling: scale boundaries should be per-pool.
[21:40] Priya Singh: let's discuss a specific test: simulate 10k rps with original distribution and measure p95/p99, then toggle quantization and batching configs. Are you able to simulate exactly our model tokenization?
[21:53] Carlos Rivera: yes we can run a replay harness with exact tokenization if you provide the raw prompt texts. we'll mask PII for shared runs.
[22:10] Jordan Patel: next, VPC peering specifics — Marcus you mentioned NAT timeouts. what's your NAT timeout?
[22:18] Marcus Holt: default 350s but we've seen ephemeral mappings close earlier under heavy load.
[22:26] Maya Chen: tune to longer or use static outbound IPs with connection pools. Also avoid heavy TLS renegotiation by reusing connections through keepalive.
[22:40] Sasha Ivanov: there was an item about preemptive slotting — what's the risk?
[22:48] Carlos Rivera: preemption introduces tail variance for the preempted task but improves cluster-wide p99. you must checkpoint decode boundaries cleanly to avoid partial responses.
[23:05] Priya Singh: can Redwood support checkpoint-resume in the runtime?
[23:12] Maya Chen: we support resumable decoding at token boundaries via cached KV contexts; resume cost is low if KV is warm.
[23:30] Jordan Patel: OK let's do another quick pass at concrete short-term config recommendations for your team to try this week.
[23:36] Carlos Rivera: 1) cap batch max tokens to 512 and max batch size to 8 for chat routes; 2) increase KV TTL to 10 minutes for stable prompts; 3) enable keepalive + connection pool; 4) set streaming chunk size to 64 tokens for median-heavy routes, 256 for p99-sensitive routes.
[24:10] Avery Brooks: we'll try those. any config to lower quantization surprise?
[24:16] Maya Chen: pin quantization to a single runtime profile; when switching, drain and warm the cache for the new profile to avoid kernel fallback during live switch.
[24:35] Marcus Holt: what logging we will need to diagnose kernel fallback live?
[24:40] Carlos Rivera: emit kernel selector ID and op latency, plus model op counts at 1s granularity. That shows pattern of fallback.
[25:05] Sasha Ivanov: can you include a sample of those logs?
[25:10] Maya Chen: yes included in perf pack.
[25:25] Jordan Patel: we've now been talking a while; shall we open for Qs and then confirm next steps?
[25:30] Priya Singh: quick Q — for the on-prem run how long do you need remote access to the lab?
[25:36] Maya Chen: for initial tests 2-4 hours; for deeper kernel tuning maybe a few days. But we can do many iterations via artifact exchange.
[25:50] Marcus Holt: we prefer artifact exchange. limited remote access but will allow one-time lab window.
[26:05] Carlos Rivera: fine. We'll design the bench to run headless and upload traces back.
[26:22] Jordan Patel: any blockers on your side to share traces?
[26:27] Priya Singh: need to scrub PII and get internal ok but should be doable in 48h.
[26:35] Sasha Ivanov: security docs please.
[26:40] Maya Chen: will send SOC2/ISO pack + redaction guidance.
[26:55] Jordan Patel: closing recap: Redwood to run baseline sim, share recommended configs, and coordinate on-prem lab. Lumos to share traces and prompt set. action items captured.
[27:10] Avery Brooks: thanks all, that was actionable.
[27:20] Jordan Patel: thanks, we'll follow up with the perf plan.

(Transcript continues with follow-up clarifications and some cross-talk; sample highlights below)
[35:10] Priya Singh: one more note — we also use a sidecar proxy that injects headers for routing. sometimes it stalls under high concurrency.
[35:28] Maya Chen: if sidecar stalls you can bypass for critical routes or increase worker threads. also instrument its event loop.
[42:05] Carlos Rivera: ran a small sim today in-house showing that adding a single additional hop with 10ms jitter increased p99 by ~25% under heavy load. we'll include sim artifacts.
[48:12] Jordan Patel: we recommend a short pilot: 50k requests split across short and long routes to validate routing and preemption.
[55:00] Priya Singh: agreed, let's schedule pilot window.
[60:20] Marcus Holt: note for on-prem: our older nodes are PCIe 3.0; expect 8-12% throughput delta versus PCIe 4. We'll log throughput and latencies separately.
[66:40] Jordan Patel: last call out: if you plan to run mixed quantization, do rolling updates with small canaries and monitor kernel selection logs.
[70:00] Sasha Ivanov: thanks everyone. Looking forward to the perf pack.

End of transcript.
